problem: Existing supervised models that predict how people perceive a navigating robot (RF, MLP, GNN on SEAN Together) are black-box and only capture correlations, so they cannot explain low perceived competence or say which controllable behavior to change. HRI data is also small.
motivation: Robots deployed around people need to anticipate perceived competence and intent so they can adapt and avoid seeming incompetent. Surveys are costly, and the largest dataset (SEAN Together, 2,964 samples) is small by ML standards. This favors a small, expert-structured causal model that supports interventions and counterfactual reasoning.
key_idea: A hand-structured Causal Bayesian Network over clustered robot trajectory features predicts perceived competence and intention. A minimal-change BFS over parent configurations of the CBN then generates counterfactual robot trajectories expected to be rated as competent.
insight: Expert-specified causal structure with time-series clustering discretization gives predictive performance at least as good as the black-box Random Forest (competence F1 0.777 vs 0.73) while using fewer features. Because it is causal, it can drive interventions. The user study shows the counterfactuals raise competence ratings (1.96 → 3.59 when the prediction was correct; 2.69 → 3.42 when it was wrong). The support threshold m=5 filters rare behaviors, but there is no ablation of it.
method: Variable preprocessing: robot-goal and human-robot (x,y) distances are collapsed into L2 norms and turned into relative changes from the start of the 8 s window, so trajectories start at 0 and stay executable. Pedestrian and map variables are dropped, leaving 7 variables (rotation change, total rotation, initial rotation, position change, human position change, competence, intention).

Generalized discretization (Alg. 1): K-means on time-series variables (cluster centroids act as intervals), quantile discretization for continuous variables, and direct values for categorical ones. At runtime a trajectory is assigned to the nearest centroid.

Expert-specified CBN: the graph is manual, with initial_robot_rotation, total_robot_rotation, robot_rotation_change and robot_pos_change as parents of competence/intention, and human_pos_change as a child of competence, intention and robot motion. Conditional probability tables are learned from data, with all variables multinomial.

Counterfactual generation (Alg. 2): BFS over parent-variable configurations with a transition matrix that allows only one variable to change by one neighbouring interval (Occam's razor). Changes to position/rotation clusters and total rotation are tried before the initial rotation. The search stops at the first configuration with P(competence=1|Pa) > ε=0.9.
Support threshold: a candidate parent configuration is considered only if it occurs more than m=5 times in the training data, which removes rare, situation-specific behaviors.

Evaluation: nested leave-one-participant-out CV (58/1/1 splits) for the number of intervals. The chosen numbers are 4 intervals each for initial and total rotation, and 10 and 11 clusters for position and rotation change. The counterfactual behavior is rendered as centroid trajectories (straight-line position toward the goal, rotation only scaled down) and tested in an online Prolific study.

setting.backbone: Causal Bayesian Network (multinomial CPTs, K-means discretization); the baseline is a Random Forest
setting.training_data: SEAN Together Robot-Following dataset: 2,964 samples from 60 participants, each with an 8 s time series and a binary competence/intention rating (Likert 1-3 → 0, 4-5 → 1)
setting.observation: 8 s time series of robot-goal distance and angle and human-robot distance (relative to the robot); pedestrian and occupancy map variables are dropped
setting.action_space: Not a control policy: it outputs counterfactual robot trajectories, i.e. cluster-centroid position change toward the goal (straight line) and rotation change, executed as video replays
setting.simulator: SEAN Together (VR social navigation, warehouse); the user study uses top-down replay videos
setting.privileged: none for prediction; the counterfactual study keeps the original human follower and pedestrian trajectories unchanged

numbers.extra: binary competence; nested LOOCV hyperparameter search
binary intention; nested LOOCV hyperparameter search

numbers.eval_set_note: 10 scenarios sampled from a 120-scenario held-out test set; 40 Prolific participants per phase; H1 phase = cases where the model correctly predicted low competence
numbers.extra: Original: 1.96 ± 0.06; Counterfactual: 3.59 ± .06 (5-point Likert); human/pedestrian trajectories not adapted
numbers.evidence: H1: 'counterfactual trajectories (3.59 ± .06) higher than the original trajectories (1.96 ± 0.06)... 83%'

numbers.eval_set_note: 10 scenarios where the model erroneously predicted low competence; 40 different participants
numbers.evidence: H2: 'counterfactual trajectories (3.42 ± .07) higher than the original trajectories (2.69 ± 0.07)... 27%'

numbers_note: Not a standard embodied-navigation benchmark; numbers are perception-prediction metrics and user-study ratings. The RF baseline is reported as F1 0.73 (competence) and 0.707 (intention).
results: The CBN beats the best RF baseline (Nav.+Facial features) in LOOCV: competence F1 0.777 vs 0.73 and accuracy 0.835 vs 0.814, and intention F1 0.751 vs 0.707. In the online study (n=40 per phase), counterfactuals raised competence ratings by 83% when the low prediction was correct (p<0.0001) and by 27% when it was erroneous.
limitations: Manually specified causal graph and manual variable selection; environment factors (walls, pedestrians) are excluded, which violates the no-unobserved-confounder assumption (one counterfactual drove the robot toward a wall).

The user study replays videos with the original human follower and pedestrian motion, since their reactions to counterfactual robot behavior cannot be predicted. It is not a live robot or VR test, and the comparison is against original behavior only, with no other counterfactual generation baseline.

Binary rating discretization and only two perceptions (competence and intention); the counterfactual is a cluster-centroid trajectory, not integrated with a motion planner. The m=5 and ε=0.9 values were set heuristically without ablation.
builds_on: Diehl et al. causal failure explanation/prevention (diehl22, diehl23)
compares_to: Random Forest (Nav. + Facial features) from SEAN Together
